report:
## Conclusion: The claim is false

Your view is correct. There is no credible scientific evidence that drinking boiled garlic water cures or treats COVID-19. This claim has been consistently and repeatedly debunked since early 2020.

**What the evidence shows:**

1. **Origin and spread of the myth**: The claim emerged early in the pandemic (around February 2020) and spread widely through social media in various forms — sometimes combined with onion, ginger, or lemon, and sometimes as a drink or inhaled steam (https://factcheck.afp.com/theres-no-scientific-proof-tonic-onions-ginger-garlic-and-lemon-can-cure-covid-19).

2. **WHO's official position**: The World Health Organization explicitly addressed this myth, stating that while garlic has some antimicrobial properties in laboratory settings, "there is no evidence from the current outbreak that eating garlic has protected people from the new coronavirus" (https://www.itv.com/news/2020-03-10/garlic-spraying-yourself-with-chlorine-and-hot-baths-do-not-prevent-coronavirus-world-health-organisation-warns).

3. **No clinical trials support it**: Searches for clinical trial evidence found no studies demonstrating garlic's efficacy against SARS-CoV-2 in humans. Existing garlic research relates to general antimicrobial lab studies (e.g., against influenza in cell cultures), not clinical outcomes for COVID-19 patients — a critical distinction, since lab/petri-dish activity does not translate to a "cure" when consumed as a drink.

4. **Repeated fact-checks worldwide**: Independent fact-checking organizations (AFP Fact Check, Rappler, various national outlets) all rated the claim "false," noting there is no official cure or preventive treatment for COVID-19 based on home remedies like garlic (https://www.rappler.com/newsbreak/fact-check/264621-heat-garlic-ginger-cure-covid-19/).

**Bottom line**: No peer-reviewed clinical evidence supports garlic water as a COVID-19 cure. The claim is a well-documented piece of pandemic-era misinformation.
